$comment: Named, owned, dated, EXPIRING exceptions to the product-separation validator.
Why this file exists: before 2026-09-10 the live validator was wired to nothing.
`npm test` ran test:product-separation (the FIXTURE test) and `npm run build` ran
validate-indexes.mjs, but neither ever ran validate-product-separation.mjs against
live index data. The detector's unit tests passed in CI on every push while the data
it exists to police had never been checked. A ninth separation failure would have
The fix is NOT to leave the guard off until the backlog is clear. Eight named, owned,
dated, expiring exceptions is a governable state; 'the validator is off' is not.
- A waived failure is reported visibly on every run. It is never silent.
- An EXPIRED waiver blocks again. Expiry is the forcing function; extending it is a
deliberate, reviewable act, not a default.
- A waiver matching nothing warns as STALE, so this list cannot rot into fiction.
- Any failure NOT matched by a live waiver blocks the build. That is the whole point.
- Waivers cover KNOWN, ADJUDICATED debt only. Never add one to silence a new finding.

waivers.reason: Three published composites for one canonical entity across two indexes: ai-labs.json '1X Technologies' (50), robotics-labs.json '1X Technologies' (81.4), robotics-labs.json 'Halodi Robotics' (62.5, the acquired entity). A 31.4-point spread on one organisation. Resolving this means deciding which index owns the entity and retiring the others, which is blocked on ratifying D-13.
waivers.remediation: Ratify D-13, then delist the non-owning rows and add redirects.

waivers.reason: ai-labs.json 'Amazon AWS AI' (35.9) and fortune-500.json 'Amazon' (12.8) — 23.1-point spread. Arguably a genuine scope distinction (an AI division vs the parent corporation) rather than a duplicate, which is precisely what D-13 must settle.
waivers.remediation: Ratify D-13. If divisional scoring is permitted, the validator's canonicalisation needs a division-aware rule rather than a waiver.

waivers.reason: SAME-index duplicate: robotics-labs.json 'Boston Dynamics' (65.6) and 'Boston Dynamics (SPOT demo)' (20.3) — 45.3-point spread. This is misfiled rather than duplicated: a DEPLOYED CONFIGURATION sitting in an organisations index, which check 3 should have caught. It surfaces through check 2 only because PARENTHETICAL_SUFFIX_RE strips '(SPOT demo)' — the same regex that is CORRECT for '(Teradyne)'. One regex, two semantics.
waivers.remediation: Not a D-13 case. Move the SPOT demo row out of the labs index into the Deployed AI Audit product, and split the regex so corporate-parent suffixes and configuration suffixes are handled differently.

waivers.reason: ai-labs.json 'Figure AI' (31.3) and robotics-labs.json 'Figure AI' (48.4) — 17.1-point spread on an identical name. The clearest true duplicate of the six: same entity, same name, two indexes, two scores.
waivers.remediation: Ratify D-13, keep the robotics-labs row (primary domain), delist the ai-labs row, redirect.

waivers.reason: ai-labs.json 'Meta AI' (26.3) and fortune-500.json 'Meta Platforms' (7.8) — 18.5-point spread. Same division-vs-parent question as Amazon.
waivers.remediation: Ratify D-13; resolve jointly with D13-amazon and D13-microsoft as one division-scoping decision.

waivers.reason: ai-labs.json 'Microsoft AI' (75.9) and fortune-500.json 'Microsoft' (65.3) — 10.6-point spread, the narrowest of the six. Division-vs-parent again.
waivers.remediation: Ratify D-13; resolve jointly with D13-amazon and D13-meta.
